technique: withholding — what the poem refuses to name or explain, and why that works
lesson:
Today we work on one thing: withholding. Withholding means the poem leaves something out on purpose and trusts you to supply it.

Notice what the poem never names. It says "same as you, / every hard thing stowed where it can be found." It never tells you what the hard thing is. It says "the cold goes honest, / clean in the lungs, no lie to it at all." It never says what the lie was. It says "There's work enough to fill the short gray day." It never names the work.

This works because your mind fills the blank with your own hard thing, your own work. The poem stays open, so you load it with what you already carry. You end up more involved than if it told you everything.

Try this: write about a worry, but never name it. Describe only what someone does around it.

The second time through, listen for how all those blanks make the last two words, "So — up!", land as a push meant for you.

Here is the poem.
poem:
A jay works the oak out past the stone wall,
hammering an acorn held tight in its foot,
that stubborn knocking the first sound of the hour —
patient, greedy, sure of the cold to come.
He's laying in against it, same as you,
every hard thing stowed where it can be found.
The grass is stiff with silver that won't last,
and smoke stands straight above the neighbor's chimney.
You pull your collar up and the cold goes honest,
clean in the lungs, no lie to it at all.
There's work enough to fill the short gray day,
but it waits — it can wait — the way good work does.

The quiet hour is yours before anything asks for you —
step into it while it's still soft and new.

So — up!
